subject: Architecture
title: Khmer Temples: Angkor Beyond the Wat
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Khmer Temples: Angkor Beyond the Wat.

hook.text: Angkor was the largest city on Earth in the 12th century — covering more area than modern Los Angeles.

buildup.text: The Khmer Empire built over 1,000 temples across Cambodia using sandstone and laterite blocks.

discovery.text: A vast water management system of reservoirs and canals supported 750,000 people in a tropical forest.

twist.text: Climate change — severe droughts followed by floods — may have caused Angkor's collapse in the 15th century.

climax.text: LIDAR scanning revealed thousands of hidden structures beneath the jungle — Angkor was far larger than thought.

punchline.text: The world's biggest city was swallowed by jungle. LIDAR found it.

quiz.question: What technology revealed hidden structures at Angkor?

details.summary: The Khmer Empire built hundreds of temples across Southeast Asia between the 9th and 15th centuries, with Angkor Wat as the most famous. But lesser-known temples like Bayon with its 216 stone faces and Ta Prohm swallowed by jungle reveal an architectural civilization of staggering ambition and.
details.whyItMatters: Angkor's temple complex shows that medieval Southeast Asia produced architecture rivaling anything in Europe. The hydraulic engineering that sustained the city's one million residents was unmatched anywhere in the medieval world.
takeaways: Hundreds of Khmer temples were built from the 9th to 15th centuries
Bayon features 216 enigmatic stone faces on its tower peaks
Angkor's hydraulic system sustained one million residents

faq.question: How big was the Angkor civilization?
faq.answer: At its peak, Angkor covered roughly 1,000 square kilometers with a population exceeding one million people. A sophisticated system of reservoirs and canals managed water supply. It was the world's largest preindustrial city, dwarfing contemporary European capitals.

faq.question: Why was Angkor abandoned?
faq.answer: Climate change disrupted the water management system, with severe droughts followed by floods damaging the reservoir network. Thai invasions, shifting trade routes, and possible social instability contributed. The population gradually relocated to Phnom Penh's area.
